q.t: Two figures are congruent when they have:
o: The same shape and the same size
q.e: Congruent figures fit exactly on top of each other — every length and every angle matches.

q.t: Which symbol means ‘is congruent to’?
q.e: ≅ combines = (same size) with ~ (same shape).

q.t: Two line segments are congruent when they have:
q.e: A segment has only one measurement — its length — so equal length means an exact fit.

q.t: Two angles are congruent when they have:
q.e: An angle is an amount of turn; how long the arms are drawn does not change it.

q.t: Two circles are congruent when they have:
q.e: A circle’s size is fixed completely by its radius.

q.t: SSS congruence means the two triangles have:
o: Two sides and an angle equal
q.e: SSS = Side-Side-Side. Three fixed side lengths can only make one triangle shape.

q.t: Which of these is NOT a rule for congruence of triangles?
q.e: Equal angles only fix the shape, not the size — a small and a large equilateral triangle both have 60°, 60°, 60°.

q.t: If △ABC ≅ △PQR, then side AB equals:
q.e: The order of letters gives the matching: A↔P, B↔Q, C↔R. So AB matches PQ.

q.t: If △ABC ≅ △PQR, then ∠B equals:
q.e: B is the second letter, so it matches the second letter Q.

q.t: Two squares are congruent when they have:
q.e: All squares already have 90° angles; only the side length can differ.

q.t: In the SAS rule, the equal angle must be:
q.e: The angle between two sides fixes how far apart their ends are. An angle elsewhere can allow two different triangles.

q.t: The RHS rule can be used only for:
q.e: RHS = Right angle, Hypotenuse, Side — it needs a right angle in each triangle.

q.t: △ABC ≅ △DEF, ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°. Find ∠F (in degrees).
q.e: ∠F matches ∠C, and ∠C = 180 − 50 − 60 = 70°.

q.t: △ABC ≅ △PQR with AB = 5 cm, BC = 7 cm and CA = 6 cm. Find QR (in cm).
q.e: QR matches BC (2nd and 3rd letters), so QR = 7 cm.

q.t: ASA congruence needs:
o: Two angles and the side between them
Two sides and the angle between them
q.e: A side with a fixed angle at each end forces the two other sides to meet at exactly one point.

q.t: If △ABC ≅ △FED, which side equals BC?
q.e: A↔F, B↔E, C↔D. So BC matches ED.

q.t: In two triangles, AB = PQ, ∠B = ∠Q and BC = QR. They are congruent by:
q.e: ∠B lies between AB and BC, and ∠Q lies between PQ and QR: two sides and the included angle.

q.t: Two right-angled triangles have equal hypotenuses and one pair of equal legs. They are congruent by:
q.e: Right angle, Hypotenuse, Side. (By Pythagoras the third sides must match too.)

q.t: △PQR ≅ △XYZ. The perimeter of △PQR is 24 cm, XY = 7 cm and YZ = 9 cm. Find XZ (in cm).
q.e: Congruent triangles have equal perimeters. XZ = 24 − 7 − 9 = 8.

q.t: Two triangles have all three angles equal. They are:
o: The same shape, but not necessarily the same size
q.e: Equal angles fix the shape only. One could be an enlargement of the other.

q.t: △ABC has AB = 4, BC = 5, AC = 6. △PQR has PQ = 5, QR = 6, PR = 4. Which statement is correct?
q.e: Match equal sides: AB = PR, BC = PQ, AC = QR. A is on AB and AC → matches R (on PR and QR). B → P, C → Q. So △ABC ≅ △RPQ.

q.t: In △ABC, AB = AC and D is the midpoint of BC. △ABD ≅ △ACD by:
q.e: AB = AC (given), BD = CD (midpoint) and AD is common to both — three pairs of sides.

q.t: In △ABC and △DEF, ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E and AB = DE. They are congruent by:
q.e: AB is the side between ∠A and ∠B; DE is between ∠D and ∠E. Two angles and the included side.

q.t: In △ABC and △DEF, AB = DE, BC = EF and ∠A = ∠D. Can we be sure they are congruent?
o: No — the angle is not between the two sides
q.e: ∠A is not between AB and BC (∠B is). Two sides and a non-included angle can make two different triangles.

q.t: A diagonal divides a rectangle into two triangles. These triangles are:
o: Similar in shape but different in size
q.e: Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal and the diagonal is common: SSS. Each triangle is exactly half the rectangle.

q.t: △ABC ≅ △PQR, ∠A = (2x + 10)° and ∠P = 70°. Find x.
Two right-angled triangles each have hypotenuse 10 cm and one leg 6 cm. What is the third side of each (in cm)?
q.e: They are congruent by RHS, and Pythagoras gives 10² − 6² = 64, so the third side is 8 cm in both.

q.t: In an isosceles triangle, the perpendicular from the vertex to the base:
o: Is longer than each equal side
Divides the base in the ratio 1 : 2
q.e: It makes two right triangles with equal hypotenuses (the equal sides) and a common leg — congruent by RHS, so the two base parts are equal.

q.t: What is the least number of matching parts needed to prove two triangles congruent?
q.e: A triangle has 6 parts (3 sides, 3 angles). The right 3 are enough — SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS — and the other 3 then follow.

q.t: CPCT stands for:
q.e: Once two triangles are proved congruent, all their remaining matching sides and angles are equal too.

q.t: △ABC ≅ △DEF. AB = (2x + 1) cm, DE = 9 cm, BC = (y + 3) cm and EF = (2y − 4) cm. Find x + y.
In △ABC, AB = AC and the bisector of ∠A meets BC at D. △ABD ≅ △ACD by:
q.e: AB = AC, ∠BAD = ∠CAD (bisector) and AD is common. The equal angle lies between the two pairs of equal sides.

q.t: △ABC ≅ △PQR, ∠A = 3x°, ∠B = 2x° and ∠R = 80°. Find ∠P (in degrees).
In quadrilateral ABCD, AB = AD and CB = CD. Diagonal AC is drawn. Which statement must be true?
q.e: △ABC ≅ △ADC by SSS (AB = AD, CB = CD, AC common). So ∠BAC = ∠DAC — AC cuts ∠A in half.

q.t: Segments AB and CD cross at O, and O is the midpoint of both. AC = 5 cm. Find BD (in cm).
q.e: OA = OB, OC = OD and ∠AOC = ∠BOD (vertically opposite), so △AOC ≅ △BOD by SAS. Matching sides: BD = AC = 5 cm.

q.t: Which information is NOT enough to prove two triangles congruent?
o: Two sides and the included angle
Two angles and the included side
q.e: Angles fix only the shape. The triangles could be different sizes.

q.t: △ABC and △DEF are right-angled at B and E. AC = DF = 13 cm and AB = DE = 5 cm. Find EF (in cm).
q.e: Congruent by RHS, so EF = BC. Pythagoras: 13² − 5² = 144, BC = 12.

q.t: Two triangles have two pairs of equal sides and one pair of equal angles. They are sure to be congruent:
o: Only if the equal angle is between the equal sides
Only if both triangles are obtuse-angled
q.e: SAS needs the included angle. With the angle elsewhere, the third side can swing to two different positions.

q.t: P is any point on the perpendicular bisector of segment AB, meeting AB at M. Then PA = PB because △PMA ≅ △PMB by:
q.e: AM = MB (bisector), ∠PMA = ∠PMB = 90° and PM is common: two sides and the angle between them.

q.t: △ABC ≅ △PQR and △PQR ≅ △XYZ. If AB = 6 cm, find XY (in cm).
q.e: AB = PQ (first congruence) and PQ = XY (second), so XY = 6 cm. Congruence passes along a chain.
